item.title: S&P/TSX composite up more than 100 points, U.S. stock markets also trade higher
item.description: Strength in base metal stocks helped Canada’s main equity index rise more than 100 points, while U.S. stock markets also climbed higher.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Strength in base metal stocks helped Canada’s main equity index rise more than 100 points in late-morning trading, while U.S. stock markets also climbed higher. The S&P/TSX composite index was up 122.97 points at 36,067.13. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 45.78 points at 52,407.36. The S&P 500 index was up 43.81 points at 7,720.58, while the Nasdaq composite was up 266.33 points at 26,435.71. The Canadian dollar traded for 71.25 cents US compared with 71.30 cents US on Monday. The December crude oil contract was down US$1.78 at US$99.98 per barrel. The December gold contract was up US$32.00 at US$4,070.40 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

item.title: Wall Street points higher in heavy week of earnings; GM heads to Nasdaq after 115 years on the NYSE
item.description: Stocks are ticking higher on Wall Street following a mixed set of profit reports from Boeing, JetBlue and other big companies.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Wall Street is ticking higher Tuesday as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry support the market, at least for now. The S&P 500 rose 0.5 per cent and pulled within 1.3 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 27 points, or 0.1 per cent, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.9 per cent higher. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 were falling, but gains for several influential AI stocks made up for that. Such stocks have been swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Broadcom climbed 3.3 per cent after announcing a US$63 billion financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions. Elsewhere in the industry, Advanced Micro Devices rose 4 per cent and was one of the strongest forces pushing up on the S&P 500 after Broadcom. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, rose 5.2 per cent, though it’s been careening between big gains and losses within each of the past few days. General Motors climbed 6.3 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it. GM began trading on the NYSE in 1911. JetBlue Airways flew 20 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least US$1 in earnings per share in 2028. Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far. Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 7.5 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year. Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among financial analysts and investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market. Boeing fell 9.4 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.8 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. It also gave a range as a forecast for profit in the final three months of the year whose midpoint fell below analysts’ expectations. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter. Sherwin-Williams fell 1.6 per cent after delivering a weaker profit than analysts expected. High mortgage rates have helped chill the housing industry, which in turn pressures demand for the paints and coatings Sherwin-Williams sells. “Customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027,” CEO Heidi Petz said. At the same time, her company is dealing with inflation pushing up its costs for raw materials. Confidence among U.S. shoppers has tumbled recently as pressure keeps building on them from high inflation. But a report on Tuesday said that U.S. consumer confidence improved in October, when economists expected further weakening. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time. The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Monday. Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.2 per cent to US$109.43. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

item.title: Cleveland-Cliffs says Stelco in full compliance, seeks meeting with minister
item.description: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. says it’s in full compliance with the promises it made as part of an Investment Canada Act review that allowed its purchase of Stelco Inc. in 2024.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CLEVELAND — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills before she will agree to meet with CEO Lourenco Goncalves. Cleveland-Cliffs says it’s in full compliance with the promises it made as part of an Investment Canada Act review that allowed its purchase of Stelco in 2024. The company also says Stelco has requested a meeting between Joly and Goncalves to talk about a path toward resuming full employment for workers who have been temporarily laid off. Joly told reporters Tuesday that the government wants a plan to bring back laid off workers before she will sit down with the head of Cleveland-Cliffs. She says the Ohio-based company has not respected its binding commitments, including a five-year commitment to maintain at least the same number of unionized workers and most non-unionized employees as when the deal was struck. Joly says Ottawa could still take the company to court to enforce its commitments, seek financial penalties or require the sale of Stelco. Cleveland-Cliffs has rejected Ottawa’s allegations, maintaining that it has met all its commitments. “The facts are clear,” Goncalves said in a statement. “We made serious commitments to Canada when we acquired Stelco, and we have honoured them.” He added that Stelco is in full compliance with all undertakings and in several important areas has even gone beyond what it committed to do. “For galvanized products, the imports of non-automotive galvanized steel that continue to flood the Canadian market remain problematic,” he said “We want to find a solution for Hamilton and its workers as soon as possible and believe common sense trade policy will make this a reality.” Joly has accused Cleveland-Cliffs of failing to honour six binding commitments made when it purchased the Ontario steelmaker. The minister has said the company must address its alleged violations, prove it has not broken its commitments or explain why it has failed to meet them. However, in a letter to Joly, the company says it’s in full compliance with each of its 34 undertakings, including its promises regarding employment levels. The company says Stelco will update its compliance report following the Oct. 31 close of the current reporting period. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

item.title: BCE sells 49.9% stake in new wireless tower company to La Caisse for $2.45B
item.description: BCE Inc. has signed a deal to sell a 49.9 per cent stake of a new company that will own and operate its wireless towers to Quebec investment manager La Caisse for $2.45 billion.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: BCE Inc. has signed a deal to sell a 49.9 per cent stake of a new company that will own and operate its wireless towers to Quebec investment manager La Caisse for $2.45 billion. The new wireless tower infrastructure company, dubbed TowerCo, will hold Bell’s portfolio of wireless infrastructure assets, with more than 5,000 sites across the country. The deal, which values the new tower company at approximately $4.91 billion, is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Under the terms of the agreement, TowerCo will lease capacity on the transferred towers to Bell, which will retain a 50.1 per cent controlling interest. Headquartered in Montreal, TowerCo will also be open to all carriers, with Bell serving as its largest customer. Bell will keep full ownership and control of its spectrum, all active network equipment and owned land. It will also maintain access to existing sites through long-term agreements, while the new company will develop new sites for Bell as needed. BCE said the new company will focus on growing the business through new site builds, site densification and third-party co-location. “This partnership unlocks the significant value embedded in our infrastructure assets while continuing to operate the award-winning wireless network our customers rely on every day,” BCE president and CEO Mirko Bibic said in a news release. “As we have consistently communicated since early 2025, our approach is to strengthen our balance sheet, invest in growth and deliver total returns to shareholders. This transaction is in keeping with that approach, and the proceeds will be used to execute against this very clear strategy.” Bell isn’t the first major telecommunication company to divest its tower infrastructure to La Caisse. Last year, Telus Corp. also sold a 49.9 per cent stake in a spun-out wireless tower operator to La Caisse for $1.26 billion. The company said the partial sale of the assets would go toward deleveraging, as part of its efforts to strengthen its balance sheet. Telus said at the time the move would also benefit the telecom industry as a whole, with other wireless carriers able to access the tower infrastructure and deliver mobile service to their customers. “A telecom tower can carry more than one network. By making this infrastructure available to different service providers, we can strengthen coverage, improve overall system efficiency, hence helping more people access the connectivity they rely on every day,” Emmanuel Jaclot, La Caisse’s executive vice-president and head of infrastructure and sustainability, said in a statement on Tuesday. “Bell’s extensive footprint and La Caisse’s global digital infrastructure expertise will give this new platform the focus and long-term perspective to grow.” Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi said he expects BCE will repurpose proceeds from the sale into areas of growth such as AI-powered solutions, at a time when the company is scaling up its investments in data centres. “We don’t see the transaction as meaningfully deleveraging the balance sheet,” he said in a note. “We expect BCE to recycle all the capital from this sale into new growth opportunities and not use the proceeds to reduce interest expense, hence we treat this deal as cash negative in the short term until new AI investments pick up the slack when completed.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026. CTV News and BNN Bloomberg are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE.
